newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian Oct output rises, but millions in poverty.
newsitem.headline: Russian Oct output rises, but millions in poverty.

text.p: Official data gave a mixed picture on Russia's economy in the first 10 months, with higher industrial output and the lowest year-on-year inflation rate since reforms began offset by hardship for millions of people.

The figures, in the November bulletin of the State Statistics Committee, showed industrial output rose seven percent in October from September, although output remained four percent below year-ago levels.
The September year-on-year fall was a steeper seven percent.
Consumer prices fell to 27.2 percent in the year to October from 31.7 percent in the year to September to mark the lowest rate since Russia launched its economic reform programme in January 1992.
The committee expected annual inflation to fall to about 23 percent by year-end if current trends continued.
The average wage also rose to 848,100 roubles in September from 831,000 in August.
But the statistics committee said 20 percent of the population, or 29.2 million people, were still receiving less than the subsistence income, although the number has been falling steadily.

A cash crunch in the Russian economy means millions of workers have not been paid for months. The committee said total wage arrears rose to 35.2 trillion roubles on October 28 from 33.22 trillion on September 23.

Despite the rise in industrial production, it remains only half of levels seen before Russia began its economic reforms. Economists said interest rates needed to fall sharply for Russia to see a lasting recovery.

"Interest rates are still far too high, dictated by those GKO yields," said United City Bank economist Christopher Granville, referring to yields of around 40 percent on short-term Russian GKO Treasury Bills.
"The central bank will not liberalise the GKO market and...unless we have cheaper money, those enterprises which have a chance cannot afford to borrow."

Other economic problems include Russia's dismal record in collecting taxes, which has forced the International Monetary Fund to delay handing over a tranche of a $10 billion three-year loan. A new IMF mission arrives in Moscow on Thursday.
Officials have said that tax collection is already high on the agenda, and Finance Mininster Alexander Livshits said the talks were difficult.
Tax evasion is rampant in Russia and the government blames firms that have not paid their taxes for wage arrears in the public sector.
But companies say the government is to blame because it has not paid for goods the firms delivered to state organisations, including the cash-strapped defence sector.

Nevertheless, many companies keep workers on though they have no orders. October unemployment was unchanged at 9.2 percent of the working population, using International Labour Organisation methods, the statistics committee said.

The head of the Federal Bankruptcy Agency said on Wednesday that Russia slightly exceeded tax revenue targets in October as debtors paid up, but Russia would launch bankruptcy proceedings against two new debtors and warned other companies to pay.
He said October tax revenues were 101 percent of planned levels. September revenues were just 48 percent of target.
($ 1 = 5,480 roubles)
--Janet Guttsman, Moscow Newsroom, +7095 941 8520
